intro_en: In this lesson you will learn to point at things. Some things are near, some are a little far, and some are far away. You will ask and answer "What is this?" and "Whose is that?". Tamil has pointing words: "இது / அது" (this / that) and "இந்த / அந்த" (this … / that …). Japanese has これ・それ・あれ and この・その・あの. The difference is that Japanese has three levels of distance. You will also learn words for things you write with, everyday objects and names of languages.

g02-1.explanation_en: There are three words for pointing at things. これ = a thing near the speaker ("this", இது). それ = a thing near the listener ("that", அது). あれ = a thing far from both of you ("that over there", அதோ அது). Today’s Tamil mostly uses only two words, "இது / அது". But Old Tamil and Sri Lankan Tamil have a middle word, "உது". That is exactly それ. These three words work like nouns. So は, も and の can come right after them: これは、それも. Say I ask 「これは 何ですか」. The listener answers 「それは ペンです」. This is because the thing near me is a little far from them.
g02-1.tamil_parallel_en: இது புத்தகம் "This is a book" / அது பேனா "That is a pen" / அதோ அது கடிகாரம் "That over there is a clock" = これは 本です。/ それは ペンです。/ あれは 時計です。 Tamil "இது / அது" match これ / それ・あれ. Japanese adds a third distance.
g02-1.formation_en: これ / それ / あれ + は + N + です
g02-1.pitfalls_en: Tamil "அது" (that) covers both それ and あれ. So remember: if it is near the listener, use それ. If it is far from both of you, use あれ. A noun can’t come right after これ・それ・あれ. 「これ本」 is wrong.

g02-2.explanation_en: これ・それ・あれ stand alone and mean "this" or "that". To say "this book" or "that pen", with a noun, use この・その・あの. Tamil changes "இது" (this) → "இந்த" (this …) and "அது" (that) → "அந்த" (that …). In the same way, Japanese changes これ → この, それ → その, あれ → あの. The distance rule is the same as before. この = near me. その = near you. あの = far from both of us. A noun must always come after この・その・あの. They never stand alone. In Tamil too, you don’t stop after just "இந்த" (this …).
g02-2.tamil_parallel_en: இந்தப் புத்தகம் என்னுடையது "This book is mine" = この本は 私のです。 Here この is roughly "இந்த" (this …). その and あの are roughly "அந்த" (that …).
g02-2.formation_en: この / その / あの + N + は …
g02-2.pitfalls_en: Putting は right after この, as in 「このは 本です」, is wrong. A noun must come after この. "This is a book" = これは 本です. "This book" = この本. Don’t mix them up.

g02-3.explanation_en: In the last lesson, の showed where someone works or studies. In this lesson it has two more jobs. First, it shows who owns something. 「私の 本」 = my book (என் புத்தகம்). 「田中さんの 傘」 = Tanaka-san’s umbrella (தனாகா-சானின் குடை). This is exactly like the Tamil "-இன் / -உடைய" (of / ’s). Second, it shows what something is about or what kind it is. 「日本語の 本」 = a Japanese-language book (ஜப்பானிய மொழிப் புத்தகம்). 「英語の 字引」 = an English dictionary (ஆங்கில அகராதி). In Tamil we just put the two words side by side here, with no ending. But in Japanese you must use の. The owner or kind always comes first. The thing comes after. This is the same order as Tamil.
g02-3.tamil_parallel_en: என் புத்தகம் "my book" / ஜப்பானிய மொழிப் புத்தகம் "Japanese-language book" = 私の 本 / 日本語の 本. Here の is roughly the Tamil "-இன் / -உடைய" (of / ’s). It also joins a kind to a thing, where Tamil just puts the two words side by side.
g02-3.pitfalls_en: Don’t write "Japanese book" as 「日本語本」 without の. "My" = 私の. Using は, as in 「私は 本」, is wrong.

g02-4.explanation_en: Someone asks a 「〜は N ですか」 question. To answer in short, without saying the noun again, use そう. 「はい、そうです」 = "Yes, that’s right / it is" (ஆமாம், அப்படித்தான் / அதுதான்). 「いいえ、そうじゃありません」 = "No, it isn’t" (இல்லை, அப்படி இல்லை). It is just like answering the Tamil "இது பேனாவா?" (Is this a pen?) with "ஆமாம், அதுதான்" (yes, that’s it). For "no", people also say 「いいえ、違います」 in place of そうじゃありません. Note: そうです is only for questions about nouns. Questions with verbs and describing words come later. 「そうですか」 with your voice going down means "I see" (அப்படியா). It shows you have understood.
g02-4.tamil_parallel_en: "இது பேனாவா?" "Is this a pen?" — "ஆமாம், அதுதான்." "Yes, it is." / "இல்லை, அப்படி இல்லை." "No, it isn’t." = 「これは ペンですか。」「はい、そうです。」/「いいえ、そうじゃありません。」 Like Tamil "அதுதான் / அப்படி இல்லை", そう takes the place of the noun.
g02-4.formation_en: はい、そうです / いいえ、そうじゃありません (= いいえ、違います)
g02-4.pitfalls_en: You can’t answer a 何 (what) question, like "What is this?", with そうです. There you must say the noun. Don’t put はい with a "no" answer, as in 「はい、そうじゃありません」.

g02-5.explanation_en: To ask "which of the two?", just say the two questions one after the other: 「これは ペンですか、鉛筆ですか」. Tamil adds "-ஆ" to both in "இது பேனாவா, பென்சிலா?" (Is this a pen or a pencil?). In the same way, Japanese puts ですか after both. You don’t need a word for "or". Don’t answer this question with はい or いいえ. Say the one you choose: 「ペンです」. In Tamil too, if someone asks "பேனாவா பென்சிலா?" (pen or pencil?), we don’t answer "ஆமாம்" (yes), right?
g02-5.tamil_parallel_en: இது பேனாவா, பென்சிலா? — பேனா. "Is this a pen or a pencil? — A pen." = これは ペンですか、鉛筆ですか。— ペンです。 Tamil puts "-ஆ" on both choices. In the same way, ですか goes on both.
g02-5.formation_en: N1 は A ですか、B ですか。 → A です / B です
g02-5.pitfalls_en: Don’t forget ですか on the second part too. 「ペンですか、鉛筆」 is wrong. The answer is not 「はい」. Say which of the two it is.

g02-6.explanation_en: "What is this?" = 「これは 何ですか」 (なん). "Whose is this?" = 「これは 誰のですか」. Here the noun after 誰の (本, かばん) is dropped. の by itself means "the one that belongs to". It is just like making Tamil "என் புத்தகம்" (my book) short → "என்னுடையது" (mine). Or "ராஜாவின் பை" (Raja’s bag) → "ராஜாவுடையது" (Raja’s). So 「私のです」 = "It’s mine" (என்னுடையது). 「田中さんのです」 = "It’s Tanaka-san’s" (தனாகா-சானுடையது). Question words (何, 誰) stay in the middle of the sentence, before です. Tamil does the same. Don’t move them to the front like in English.
g02-6.tamil_parallel_en: இது யாருடையது? — என்னுடையது. "Whose is this? — It’s mine." = これは 誰のですか。— 私のです。 Here の is roughly the Tamil "-உடையது" (the one that belongs to).
g02-6.formation_en: N は 何ですか ; N は 誰のですか → (person) のです
g02-6.pitfalls_en: 「誰ですか」 = "Who?" (யார்?). 「誰のですか」 = "Whose?" (யாருடையது?). If you drop の, the meaning changes. Before です, 何 is read なん (not なに).

g02-7.explanation_en: Put お before some nouns that belong to someone else. This makes them polite. お名前 = your name (உங்கள் பெயர்). お国 = your country (உங்கள் நாடு). It is like adding "தங்கள்" (your, with respect) in Tamil: "பெயர்" (name) → "தங்கள் பெயர்", "ஊர்" (hometown) → "தங்கள் ஊர்". Important rule: never use お when you talk about yourself. Say 「私の 名前は ラジャです」. 私の お名前 is wrong. You can’t put お before every word. Only some common words take it (お名前、お国、おいくつ). Katakana words (カメラ, ペン) don’t take お.
g02-7.tamil_parallel_en: தங்கள் பெயர்? "Your name?" / தங்கள் நாடு? "Your country?" = お名前は？ / お国は？ Here お works like the polite Tamil "தங்கள்" (your).
g02-7.formation_en: お + N (someone else’s) ; no お for your own
g02-7.pitfalls_en: 「私の お名前」 is wrong. Don’t put お on your own things. お is not a separate word. Write it joined to the noun (おなまえ).

items.L02-q01: 時計 = とけい (கடிகாரம், clock / watch). It ends with the long sound けい. Making it short, as とけ, is wrong. Changing the sound to どけい is also wrong.
items.L02-q02: 英語 = えいご (ஆங்கிலம், English). 語 is ご (not こ). Don’t make the long sound えい short, as えご.
items.L02-q03: 鉛筆 = えんぴつ (பென்சில், pencil). 筆 alone is ひつ. But after 鉛 it changes to ぴつ. えんひつ and えんびつ are wrong.
items.L02-q04: かさ = 傘 (குடை, umbrella). 金, 全 and 命 look like it. They all have a 人 shape on top. But 傘 has four small 人 inside.
items.L02-q05: ほん = 本 (புத்தகம், book). Add a short line at the bottom of 木 (மரம், tree), and you get 本. 体 and 休 also have 木 in them, but they are different characters.
items.L02-q06: The answer uses それ (the thing near you). So the question uses これ (the thing near me). この / その / あの need a noun after them. は can’t come right after them.
items.L02-q07: The answer is "mine". So the question is "whose" = 誰の (யாருடைய). With なん (என்ன, what), the answer would be a thing.
items.L02-q08: カメラ (camera) is a word written in katakana. In hiragana it would be かめら.
items.L02-q09: Only a dictionary (字引, அகராதி) can be "… of the Japanese language". A key, an umbrella and a clock don’t have a language.
items.L02-q10: The question asks about a noun: "Is it a pen?". "Yes, it is" = はい、そうです. あれ is the pointing word "that over there" (அதோ அது). It doesn’t fit here.
items.L02-q11: Only あの (அந்த, that …) can come before the noun 人. あれ / それ / これ are pointing words that stand alone. They don’t come before a noun.
items.L02-q12: "This book is mine" = "This is my book" (இது என் புத்தகம்). 本 is dropped after 私の. The first choice says "not".
items.L02-q13: そうじゃありません = "it isn’t" (அப்படி இல்லை). So "that is not a pencil" (பென்சில் இல்லை). "That is a pencil too" (も) is the opposite.
items.L02-q14: 山田さんの = "Yamada-san’s" (யமாடா-சானுடையது). The dropped noun is 時計 (clock). "Yamada-san is a clock" makes no sense.
items.L02-q15: The pointing word これ is the topic, so use は. With の, the meaning changes to "this one’s bag". Then the sentence doesn’t finish.
items.L02-q16: Before the noun 本, use この (இந்த, this …). これ (இது, this) only stands alone. 「これ本」 is wrong.
items.L02-q17: "English dictionary" (ஆங்கில அகராதி) uses の to join a kind to a thing. は is not used twice in one sentence.
items.L02-q18: The person asking says それ (near you). So for the person answering, it is これ (near me). The distance word changes with who is speaking.
items.L02-q19: "Is it Tanaka-san’s?" (தனாகா-சானுடையதா?) = 田中さんのですか. の gives the meaning "belonging to". は would make two は in one sentence.
items.L02-q20: In an "A or B?" question, the second part needs か too. も gives a different meaning: "a pencil too".
items.L02-q21: It starts with いいえ, so the answer is "no". 私のじゃありません = "It’s not mine" (என்னுடையது இல்லை). です would not agree with いいえ.
items.L02-q22: これは 私の 日本語の 本です。 — owner (私の) → kind (日本語の) → thing (本). 日本語の goes in the ★ slot.
items.L02-q23: そのかばんは 誰のですか。 — その comes before the noun. 誰の comes before です. 誰の goes in the ★ slot.
items.L02-q24: あれは ペンですか、鉛筆ですか。 — both choices take ですか. 鉛筆 goes in the ★ slot.
items.L02-q25: ［1］ "Japanese-language teacher" (ஜப்பானிய மொழி ஆசிரியர்) uses の to join a kind to a person. ［2］ "Not the teacher’s, it’s mine" = 私のです. Here の means "belonging to". ［3］ The second か of an "A or B?" question.
